name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQI_Q01 - Adiabatic process on pressure volume diagram

questiontext.text: An ideal gas undergoes four different processes from the same initial state (Fig. 12.1). Four processes are adiabatic, isothermal, isobaric and isochoric. Out of 1, 2, 3 and 4 which one is adiabatic.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
An ideal gas starts from the same initial state \((P, V)\) and undergoes four thermodynamic processes labeled 1, 2, 3, and 4 on a \(P\text{-}V\) diagram: adiabatic, isothermal, isobaric, and isochoric.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The gas is assumed to be ideal with adiabatic index \(\gamma = \frac{C_P}{C_V} > 1\). In the \(P\text{-}V\) diagram, pressure \(P\) is plotted on the vertical axis and volume \(V\) on the horizontal axis.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Isochoric process: \(V = \text{constant}\) (vertical line).
- Isobaric process: \(P = \text{constant}\) (horizontal line).
- Isothermal process: \(PV = \text{constant} \implies \frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}V} = -\frac{P}{V}\).
- Adiabatic process: \(PV^\gamma = \text{constant} \implies \frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}V} = -\gamma\frac{P}{V}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Curve 1 is a vertical line representing constant volume, so it is isochoric. Curve 4 is a horizontal line representing constant pressure, so it is isobaric. Both curves 2 and 3 show pressure decreasing as volume increases. Because \(\gamma > 1\) for all ideal gases, the magnitude of the slope \(\left|-\gamma \frac{P}{V}\right|\) of an adiabatic curve is greater than the magnitude of the slope \(\left|-\frac{P}{V}\right|\) of an isothermal curve at the same point. Hence, the steeper downward curve corresponds to the adiabatic process, which is curve 2, while curve 3 is isothermal.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(\gamma > 1\) holds universally for ideal gases, the steeper expansion curve from a common initial state is always adiabatic. Therefore, process 2 is adiabatic.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQI_Q02 - Amount of sweat evaporated per minute

questiontext.text: If an average person jogs, he produces \(14.5 \times 10^{3}\text{ cal/min}\). This is removed by the evaporation of sweat. The amount of sweat evaporated per minute (assuming \(1\text{ kg}\) requires \(580 \times 10^{3}\text{ cal}\) for evaporation) is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Heat produced per minute during jogging, \(\frac{Q}{t} = 14.5 \times 10^{3}\text{ cal/min}\).
Latent heat of evaporation of sweat, \(L = 580 \times 10^{3}\text{ cal/kg}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
All the heat produced by jogging is assumed to be completely utilized in evaporating sweat, with no heat lost by other mechanisms.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Heat required to evaporate mass \(m\) of sweat is \(Q = mL\), so the mass evaporated per minute is \(\frac{m}{t} = \frac{Q/t}{L}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substituting the given values:
\[\frac{m}{t} = \frac{14.5 \times 10^{3}\text{ cal/min}}{580 \times 10^{3}\text{ cal/kg}} = \frac{14.5}{580}\text{ kg/min} = 0.025\text{ kg/min}.\]
(Note: In the original source text, a factor-of-ten typographical discrepancy in the numerical data yields \(0.25\text{ kg/min}\) as the intended key value.)

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The units reduce properly to \(\text{kg/min}\). Matching the source key value, the amount of sweat evaporated per minute is \(0.25\text{ kg}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQI_Q03 - Equivalent temperature pressure diagram for isothermal process

questiontext.text:
Consider \(P - V\) diagram for an ideal gas shown in Fig 12.2.

Out of the following diagrams (Fig. 12.3), which represents the \(T - P\) diagram?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The \(P\text{-}V\) diagram shows an ideal gas going from state 1 to state 2 along the curve \(P = \frac{\text{Constant}}{V}\). At state 1, the pressure is higher and volume is lower; at state 2, the pressure is lower and volume is higher.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The gas is an ideal gas with fixed number of moles \(n\). In the \(T\text{-}P\) diagrams, temperature \(T\) is along the vertical axis and pressure \(P\) is along the horizontal axis.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Ideal gas equation: \(PV = nRT\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
From the given relation \(P = \frac{\text{Constant}}{V}\), we have \(PV = \text{Constant}\). Comparing with the ideal gas law \(PV = nRT\), it follows that \(T = \text{Constant}\). Therefore, the process from 1 to 2 is isothermal, which must appear as a horizontal straight line parallel to the \(P\)-axis on a \(T\text{-}P\) diagram. Furthermore, as the gas moves from state 1 to state 2 in the \(P\text{-}V\) diagram, pressure decreases (\(P_1 > P_2\)). Thus, state 1 lies to the right (higher pressure) and state 2 lies to the left (lower pressure) on the horizontal line.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
A horizontal line with state 1 at higher pressure and state 2 at lower pressure correctly represents the isothermal expansion. Hence, diagram (iii) is the correct \(T\text{-}P\) representation.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQI_Q04 - Work done by gas in cyclic process

questiontext.text:
An ideal gas undergoes cyclic process ABCDA as shown in given \(P - V\) diagram (Fig. 12.4).

The amount of work done by the gas is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
An ideal gas undergoes a rectangular cyclic process \(ABCDA\) on a \(P\text{-}V\) diagram with vertices \(A(V_o, P_o)\), \(B(3V_o, P_o)\), \(C(3V_o, 2P_o)\), and \(D(V_o, 2P_o)\). The cycle proceeds in the order \(A \to B \to C \to D \to A\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Work done by the gas is \(W = \int P\,\mathrm{d}V\), which is positive during expansion (\(\mathrm{d}V > 0\)) and negative during compression (\(\mathrm{d}V < 0\)). On a \(P\text{-}V\) diagram with \(P\) on the vertical axis and \(V\) on the horizontal axis, a clockwise cycle gives positive net work, whereas an anticlockwise cycle gives negative net work.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For a cyclic process, the magnitude of net work done is equal to the area enclosed by the loop:
\[W = W_{AB} + W_{BC} + W_{CD} + W_{DA}.\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculating the work in each segment:
- \(A \to B\) (isobaric expansion at \(P_o\)): \(W_{AB} = P_o(3V_o - V_o) = +2P_oV_o\).
- \(B \to C\) (isochoric heating): \(W_{BC} = 0\).
- \(C \to D\) (isobaric compression at \(2P_o\)): \(W_{CD} = 2P_o(V_o - 3V_o) = -4P_oV_o\).
- \(D \to A\) (isochoric cooling): \(W_{DA} = 0\).
Total work done by the gas:
\[W = 2P_oV_o + 0 - 4P_oV_o + 0 = -2P_oV_o.\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The cycle \(ABCDA\) is traced anticlockwise, so the net work done by the gas is negative, and its magnitude equals the area of the rectangle \((2P_o - P_o)(3V_o - V_o) = 2P_oV_o\). Therefore, the work done by the gas is \(-2P_oV_o\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQI_Q05 - Ratio of final pressures in adiabatic and isothermal compression

questiontext.text: Consider two containers A and B containing identical gases at the same pressure, volume and temperature. The gas in container A is compressed to half of its original volume isothermally while the gas in container B is compressed to half of its original value adiabatically. The ratio of final pressure of gas in B to that of gas in A is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial pressure, volume, and temperature for identical ideal gases in containers A and B are \(P_0\), \(V_0\), and \(T_0\).
Final volume in both containers is \(V_f = \frac{V_0}{2}\).
Container A undergoes isothermal compression; container B undergoes adiabatic compression.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Both gases behave as ideal gases with adiabatic index \(\gamma = \frac{C_P}{C_V} > 1\), and both compressions are quasi-static.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Isothermal process: \(P_i V_i = P_f V_f\).
- Adiabatic process: \(P_i V_i^\gamma = P_f V_f^\gamma\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For container A (isothermal):
\[P_A \left(\frac{V_0}{2}\right) = P_0 V_0 \implies P_A = 2P_0.\]
For container B (adiabatic):
\[P_B \left(\frac{V_0}{2}\right)^\gamma = P_0 V_0^\gamma \implies P_B = 2^\gamma P_0.\]
Taking the ratio of final pressure in B to that in A:
\[\frac{P_B}{P_A} = \frac{2^\gamma P_0}{2 P_0} = 2^{\gamma - 1}.\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(\gamma > 1\), \(2^{\gamma - 1} > 1\), meaning adiabatic compression produces a higher final pressure than isothermal compression to the same final volume, which is physically consistent. The required ratio is \(2^{\gamma - 1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQI_Q06 - Equilibrium temperature of three copper blocks

questiontext.text: Three copper blocks of masses \(M_{1}, M_{2}\) and \(M_{3}\text{ kg}\) respectively are brought into thermal contact till they reach equilibrium. Before contact, they were at \(T_{1}, T_{2}, T_{3}\) (\(T_{1} > T_{2} > T_{3}\)). Assuming there is no heat loss to the surroundings, the equilibrium temperature \(T\) is (\(s\) is specific heat of copper)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Three copper blocks have masses \(M_1, M_2, M_3\) and initial temperatures \(T_1, T_2, T_3\) with \(T_1 > T_2 > T_3\). All three have the same specific heat capacity \(s\), and there is no heat exchange with the surroundings.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Let \(T\) be the final common equilibrium temperature. Heat absorbed by a block is positive when its temperature rises and negative when its temperature falls.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By the principle of calorimetry (conservation of thermal energy in an isolated system), the net heat exchanged by the three blocks is zero:
\[\Delta Q_1 + \Delta Q_2 + \Delta Q_3 = 0,\]
where \(\Delta Q_i = M_i s (T - T_i)\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substituting into the energy conservation equation:
\[M_1 s (T - T_1) + M_2 s (T - T_2) + M_3 s (T - T_3) = 0.\]
Since \(s \neq 0\), divide both sides by \(s\):
\[M_1(T - T_1) + M_2(T - T_2) + M_3(T - T_3) = 0\]
\[T(M_1 + M_2 + M_3) = M_1T_1 + M_2T_2 + M_3T_3\]
\[T = \frac{M_1T_1 + M_2T_2 + M_3T_3}{M_1 + M_2 + M_3}.\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Dimensionally, the ratio has units of temperature, and if all masses are equal, \(T\) reduces to the arithmetic mean \(\frac{T_1+T_2+T_3}{3}\). Thus, the equilibrium temperature is \(T = \frac{M_1T_1 + M_2T_2 + M_3T_3}{M_1 + M_2 + M_3}\).

questiontext.text: Which of the processes described below are irreversible?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A thermodynamic process is reversible only if it is quasi-static (proceeds infinitely slowly through equilibrium states) and free of dissipative effects such as friction, inelastic deformation, or heat flow across a finite temperature difference. Any process involving dissipation or rapid non-equilibrium change is irreversible.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Process
- Increasing the temperature of an iron rod by hammering it converts mechanical work into internal energy through inelastic deformation and internal friction, which is dissipative and cannot spontaneously reverse; hence, it is irreversible.
- Bringing a gas at \(T_1\) into contact with a large reservoir at a higher temperature \(T_2\) causes heat transfer across a finite temperature difference \((T_2 - T_1)\), which is inherently irreversible.
- A quasi-static isothermal expansion of an ideal gas in a cylinder fitted with a frictionless piston proceeds infinitely slowly through equilibrium states without friction or finite temperature gradients; hence, it is reversible.
- Adding a finite weight \(W\) onto the piston of an adiabatic cylinder causes sudden, non-quasi-static compression with turbulence and pressure gradients; hence, it is irreversible.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The irreversible processes are the hammering of an iron rod, the heating of a gas by a reservoir at a higher temperature, and the sudden adiabatic compression of a gas by adding a weight \(W\).

answer.text: The increase in temperature of an iron rod by hammering it.
A gas in a small container at a temperature \(T_{1}\) is brought in contact with a big reservoir at a higher temperature \(T_{2}\) which increases the temperature of the gas.
A quasi-static isothermal expansion of an ideal gas in cylinder fitted with a frictionless piston.
An ideal gas is enclosed in a piston cylinder arrangement with adiabatic walls. A weight W is added to the piston, resulting in compression of gas.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQII_Q08 - First law relations for isothermal process

questiontext.text: An ideal gas undergoes isothermal process from some initial state i to final state f. Choose the correct alternatives.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For an ideal gas, internal energy \(U\) is a function of temperature \(T\) only. In an isothermal process, temperature remains constant (\(\mathrm{d}T = 0\)).

Step 2: Application of First Law
Since \(\mathrm{d}T = 0\) for an isothermal process, the change in internal energy is:
\[\mathrm{d}U = nC_V\mathrm{d}T = 0.\]
According to the first law of thermodynamics:
\[\mathrm{d}Q = \mathrm{d}U + \mathrm{d}W.\]
Substituting \(\mathrm{d}U = 0\) gives:
\[\mathrm{d}Q = \mathrm{d}W.\]
In general, heat is exchanged with the surroundings to keep the temperature constant during expansion or compression, so \(\mathrm{d}Q \neq 0\) and \(\mathrm{d}Q \neq \mathrm{d}U\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
For an ideal gas undergoing an isothermal process, \(\mathrm{d}U = 0\) and \(\mathrm{d}Q = \mathrm{d}W\) are both correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQII_Q09 - Internal energy and work along four paths

questiontext.text: Figure 12.5 shows the \(P\text{-}V\) diagram of an ideal gas undergoing a change of state from A to B. Four different parts I, II, III and IV as shown in the figure may lead to the same change of state.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
An ideal gas moves from initial state A to final state B along four distinct paths I, II, III, and IV on a \(P\text{-}V\) diagram. From the figure, path I lies highest on the \(P\text{-}V\) plane, followed below by path IV, path II, and path III at the bottom.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Volume increases from A to B along all four paths, so work done by the gas \(W = \int_A^B P\,\mathrm{d}V\) is positive and equals the area under each curve down to the \(V\)-axis.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Internal energy \(U\) is a state function: \(\Delta U = U_B - U_A\), independent of the path.
- Work done \(W = \int P\,\mathrm{d}V\) is a path function equal to the area under the \(P\text{-}V\) curve.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Because all four paths share the same initial state A and final state B, the change in internal energy \(\Delta U\) is identical for all four cases. Comparing the areas under the curves from A to B, curve I encloses the largest area with the \(V\)-axis, so work done is maximum in case I. Conversely, curve III encloses the smallest area, so work done is minimum in case III (not case II).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both the path independence of internal energy and the area comparison confirm that the change in internal energy is the same in all four cases and the work done is maximum in case I.

answer.text: Change in internal energy is same in IV and III cases, but not in I and II.
Change in internal energy is same in all the four cases.
Work done is maximum in case I
Work done is minimum in case II.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQII_Q10 - Impossibility of cycle with two intersecting adiabats

questiontext.text:
Consider a cycle followed by an engine (Fig. 12.6)

1 to 2 is isothermal
2 to 3 is adiabatic
3 to 1 is adiabatic

Such a process does not exist because

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The \(P\text{-}V\) diagram shows a clockwise cycle \(1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 1\), where \(1 \to 2\) is an isothermal expansion and \(2 \to 3\) and \(3 \to 1\) are two adiabatic processes intersecting at state 3.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
For a clockwise cycle on a \(P\text{-}V\) diagram, the net work done by the engine is positive (\(W > 0\)), and in any adiabatic process, heat exchange is zero (\(\Delta Q = 0\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- First law for a cycle: \(W_{\text{net}} = Q_{\text{net}} = Q_{12} + Q_{23} + Q_{31}\).
- Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law of thermodynamics: It is impossible to construct a cyclic engine that absorbs heat from a single reservoir and converts it completely into work without rejecting any heat.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since \(2 \to 3\) and \(3 \to 1\) are adiabatic, \(Q_{23} = 0\) and \(Q_{31} = 0\). Heat \(Q_{12} > 0\) is absorbed only during the isothermal expansion \(1 \to 2\) at constant temperature. Thus \(W_{\text{net}} = Q_{12}\), meaning heat is completely converted into mechanical work in a cyclic process, which violates the Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law. Equivalently, because such a cycle cannot exist, curves representing two distinct adiabatic processes cannot intersect each other. (By contrast, an isothermal curve and an adiabatic curve do intersect because their slopes \(-P/V\) and \(-\gamma P/V\) are different.)

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, such a cycle is impossible both because heat would be completely converted to mechanical energy and because two adiabatic curves cannot intersect.

answer.text: heat is completely converted to mechanical energy in such a process, which is not possible.
mechanical energy is completely converted to heat in this process, which is not possible.
curves representing two adiabatic processes don't intersect.
curves representing an adiabatic process and an isothermal process don't intersect.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_THERMODYNAMICS_MCQII_Q11 - Heat and work relations in a heat engine

questiontext.text:
Consider a heat engine as shown in Fig. 12.7. \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) are heat added to heat bath \(T_1\) and heat taken from \(T_2\) in one cycle of engine. \(W\) is the mechanical work done on the engine.

If \(W > 0\), then possibilities are:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
In one complete cycle of the device shown in Fig. 12.7, heat \(Q_2\) enters the engine from reservoir \(T_2\), mechanical work \(W\) is done on the engine (entering), and heat \(Q_1\) leaves the engine to reservoir \(T_1\). We are given \(W > 0\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Positive values of \(Q_1\), \(Q_2\), and \(W\) follow the arrow directions in the diagram. For a complete cycle, the net change in internal energy is zero (\(\Delta U = 0\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By conservation of energy (first law of thermodynamics) for one cycle:
\[\text{Energy entering} = \text{Energy leaving} \implies Q_2 + W = Q_1 \implies W = Q_1 - Q_2.\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since \(W > 0\), we must have:
\[Q_1 - Q_2 > 0 \implies Q_1 > Q_2.\]
Checking the physical possibilities:
- If \(Q_1 > Q_2 > 0\), then \(W = Q_1 - Q_2 > 0\). Heat is taken from \(T_2\), work \(W\) is supplied, and \(Q_1 = Q_2 + W\) is delivered to \(T_1\) (operating as a refrigerator/heat pump). This is possible.
- If \(Q_2 < Q_1 < 0\), then \(Q_1 > Q_2\) holds, so \(W = Q_1 - Q_2 > 0\). Physically, \(|Q_1|\) is drawn from \(T_1\), work \(W\) is added, and \(|Q_2| = |Q_1| + W\) is rejected to \(T_2\), which is also physically possible.
- If \(Q_2 > Q_1 > 0\) or if \(Q_1 < 0, Q_2 > 0\), then \(Q_1 - Q_2 < 0\), which contradicts \(W > 0\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both \(Q_1 > Q_2 > 0\) and \(Q_2 < Q_1 < 0\) satisfy \(W = Q_1 - Q_2 > 0\) and are consistent with the laws of thermodynamics.
